questions.stem_html: A 23-year-old man is evaluated after his father has a myocardial infarction at age 41. Examination shows firm nodules over both Achilles tendons. His fasting triglyceride level is normal, but LDL cholesterol is 318 mg/dL. The accompanying diagram shows uptake of an apoB-100-containing particle by a hepatocyte. Which cellular process is most likely impaired?

options.text_html: Transfer of cholesterol ester from HDL to VLDL by CETP
Receptor-mediated endocytosis of LDL followed by receptor recycling
Hydrolysis of triglycerides in chylomicrons by lipoprotein lipase
Assembly of apoB-48-containing particles in intestinal enterocytes
ABCA1-mediated export of cellular cholesterol to nascent HDL

questions.explanation_html: Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia most often results from defective LDL-receptor function. Reduced hepatic binding and endocytosis of apoB-100-containing LDL decreases plasma LDL clearance, causing markedly elevated LDL, tendon xanthomas, and premature atherosclerosis.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: CETP exchanges lipids between HDL and apoB-containing lipoproteins but does not produce this classic isolated LDL phenotype.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency causes severe hypertriglyceridemia and pancreatitis.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: ApoB-48 is required for intestinal chylomicron formation, not hepatic LDL clearance.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: ABCA1 loss causes Tangier disease with very low HDL and cholesterol-laden tissues.

questions.educational_objective: Familial hypercholesterolemia causes isolated severe LDL elevation through impaired hepatic LDL-receptor binding, endocytosis, or recycling.

media.alt_text: Original hepatocyte diagram showing LDL receptor binding, endocytosis, lysosomal processing, and receptor recycling.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
GeneReviews. Familial Hypercholesterolemia. NCBI Bookshelf.

taxonomy.subtopic: Pulmonary vascular remodeling and Eisenmenger shunt reversal

questions.stem_html: A 32-year-old woman with an unrepaired large ventricular septal defect develops exertional dyspnea, clubbing, cyanosis, and secondary erythrocytosis. The accompanying pressure-flow diagram contrasts her childhood circulation with her current circulation. Which change most directly caused the reversal of blood flow across the defect?

options.text_html: Progressive reduction in systemic vascular resistance
Closure of the ductus arteriosus after birth
Increased left ventricular compliance
Pulmonary vascular remodeling that raises pulmonary vascular resistance above systemic resistance
Development of severe mitral regurgitation

questions.explanation_html: A large VSD initially produces a left-to-right shunt because systemic pressure exceeds pulmonary pressure. Chronic pulmonary overcirculation causes endothelial dysfunction, medial hypertrophy, and intimal proliferation. When pulmonary vascular resistance exceeds systemic resistance, the shunt reverses and deoxygenated blood enters the systemic circulation.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Lower systemic resistance can transiently favor right-to-left flow but is not the chronic structural cause of Eisenmenger physiology.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Ductal closure does not explain reversal across a ventricular defect years later.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Left ventricular compliance is not the primary determinant of the acquired pulmonary hypertension.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Mitral regurgitation does not produce the pulmonary arteriolar remodeling characteristic of Eisenmenger syndrome.

questions.educational_objective: Eisenmenger syndrome results when chronic high-flow left-to-right shunting produces irreversible pulmonary vascular remodeling and right-to-left reversal.

media.alt_text: Original diagram comparing early left-to-right VSD flow with late right-to-left Eisenmenger flow.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
AHA/ACC Guideline for the Management of Adults With Congenital Heart Disease.

taxonomy.subtopic: Intercostal collateral circulation and rib notching

questions.stem_html: A 19-year-old man has headaches, upper-extremity hypertension, weak delayed femoral pulses, and a systolic murmur over the back. Chest imaging shows bilateral inferior rib notching. The accompanying vascular map shows collateral vessels bypassing a narrowed descending aorta. Enlargement of which arteries most directly produces the rib finding?

options.text_html: Posterior intercostal arteries supplied through subclavian and internal thoracic collaterals
Superior epigastric arteries supplied by the external iliac arteries
Bronchial arteries supplied directly from the pulmonary trunk
Coronary arteries supplied by the ascending aorta
Inferior phrenic arteries supplied by the celiac trunk

questions.explanation_html: In postductal coarctation, collateral blood travels from the subclavian system through internal thoracic and intercostal pathways to the descending aorta. Enlarged tortuous intercostal arteries erode the inferior margins of the ribs, producing rib notching.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: The superior epigastric arteries arise from the internal thoracic arteries and do not course along the rib undersurfaces.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Bronchial arteries do not create the classic intercostal rib erosion.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Coronary enlargement is not responsible for rib notching.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Inferior phrenic arteries do not form the characteristic thoracic collateral pathway.

questions.educational_objective: Postductal coarctation causes inferior rib notching through enlargement of collateral intercostal arteries connecting proximal subclavian circulation with the distal aorta.

media.alt_text: Original arterial map showing subclavian, internal thoracic, intercostal, and distal aortic collateral flow.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease.

questions.stem_html: A 6-year-old boy develops periorbital edema after a mild respiratory illness. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein without blood, and serum albumin is low. The accompanying panel shows normal glomeruli by light microscopy, no immune deposits by immunofluorescence, and a change on electron microscopy. Which ultrastructural finding is most likely?

options.text_html: Subendothelial immune-complex deposits with duplication of the basement membrane
Mesangial electron-dense deposits
Linear deposition of IgG along the basement membrane
Subepithelial deposits separated by basement-membrane spikes
Diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes

questions.explanation_html: Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in young children. Light microscopy is typically normal, immunofluorescence is negative, and electron microscopy demonstrates diffuse podocyte foot-process effacement caused by altered glomerular permeability.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Subendothelial deposits and basement-membrane duplication suggest membranoproliferative patterns.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Mesangial deposits are characteristic of IgA nephropathy.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Linear IgG staining is typical of anti-GBM disease.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Subepithelial spike-and-dome deposits indicate membranous nephropathy.

questions.educational_objective: Minimal change disease presents with selective nephrotic proteinuria and diffuse podocyte foot-process effacement despite normal light microscopy and negative immunofluorescence.

media.alt_text: Original light microscopy, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy comparison for minimal change disease.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular Diseases.

questions.stem_html: A 24-year-old man develops gross hematuria one day after the onset of pharyngitis. Complement levels are normal. Kidney biopsy shows mesangial proliferation and dominant mesangial IgA staining. The accompanying pathway begins with production of abnormally glycosylated IgA1. Which subsequent event most directly produces glomerular injury?

options.text_html: Formation of antibodies against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen
Deposition of circulating cryoglobulins in subendothelial locations
Formation and mesangial deposition of immune complexes containing galactose-deficient IgA1
Activation of complement by antibodies against phospholipase A2 receptor
T-cell-mediated loss of podocyte slit-diaphragm charge

questions.explanation_html: IgA nephropathy follows a multihit mechanism: galactose-deficient IgA1 is produced, antiglycan antibodies form, circulating immune complexes develop, and these complexes deposit in the mesangium, activating inflammatory pathways and causing synpharyngitic hematuria.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Anti-type IV collagen antibodies cause anti-GBM disease.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Cryoglobulinemia usually produces a membranoproliferative pattern and low complement.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Anti-PLA2R antibodies are associated with primary membranous nephropathy.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Podocyte permeability changes without immune deposits characterize minimal change disease.

questions.educational_objective: IgA nephropathy results from mesangial deposition of immune complexes containing galactose-deficient IgA1 and antiglycan antibodies.

media.alt_text: Original four-hit pathway from galactose-deficient IgA1 production to mesangial immune-complex deposition.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
Suzuki H et al. The pathophysiology of IgA nephropathy. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology.

questions.stem_html: A 67-year-old man with diabetic kidney disease takes lisinopril. Laboratory studies show potassium 6.0 mEq/L, bicarbonate 17 mEq/L, and a normal serum anion gap. Urine pH is 5.1. The accompanying nephron diagram shows reduced aldosterone signaling. Which additional change is most responsible for the metabolic acidosis?

options.text_html: Increased proximal bicarbonate wasting
Impaired apical hydrogen secretion despite severe hypokalemia
Increased distal sodium delivery with enhanced potassium secretion
Reduced ammoniagenesis and urinary ammonium excretion caused by hyperkalemia
Increased generation of titratable acid from filtered phosphate

questions.explanation_html: Type IV RTA is caused by deficient aldosterone effect. Reduced distal sodium reabsorption lowers potassium and hydrogen secretion, while hyperkalemia suppresses proximal ammoniagenesis. Low urinary ammonium limits net acid excretion even when urine pH can fall below 5.5.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Proximal bicarbonate wasting causes type II RTA and usually hypokalemia.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Distal hydrogen-secretory failure causes type I RTA and an inappropriately high urine pH.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Aldosterone deficiency reduces rather than enhances distal potassium secretion.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Increased titratable-acid generation would improve, not impair, net acid excretion.

questions.educational_objective: Hyperkalemic type IV RTA reflects reduced aldosterone effect and hyperkalemia-mediated suppression of renal ammonium production and excretion.

media.alt_text: Original nephron diagram linking low aldosterone effect, hyperkalemia, reduced ammoniagenesis, and low urinary ammonium.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
Palmer BF, Clegg DJ. Hyperkalemic renal tubular acidosis. Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology.

questions.stem_html: An 8-year-old boy has recurrent painful knee swelling after minor trauma. Platelet count and bleeding time are normal. Prothrombin time is normal, and activated partial thromboplastin time is prolonged but corrects after mixing with normal plasma. The accompanying coagulation diagram highlights the intrinsic tenase complex. Deficiency of which function best explains these findings?

options.text_html: Cofactor activity that permits factor IXa to efficiently activate factor X
Platelet adhesion to exposed subendothelial collagen
Gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, and X
Conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin by thrombin
Inhibition of plasmin by alpha-2-antiplasmin

questions.explanation_html: Factor VIIIa serves as a cofactor for factor IXa in the intrinsic tenase complex, greatly accelerating factor X activation. Hemophilia A causes deep tissue and joint bleeding, an isolated prolonged aPTT, and correction on mixing when no inhibitor is present.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Defective platelet adhesion describes von Willebrand disease and causes mucocutaneous bleeding.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Impaired gamma-carboxylation affects both PT and aPTT and multiple vitamin K-dependent factors.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Thrombin directly converts fibrinogen to fibrin but is not selectively deficient in hemophilia A.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Alpha-2-antiplasmin deficiency causes excessive fibrinolysis rather than an isolated intrinsic-pathway defect.

questions.educational_objective: Factor VIII is the cofactor for factor IXa in intrinsic tenase; its deficiency causes hemarthroses and a mixing-correctable isolated prolonged aPTT.

media.alt_text: Original mixing-study graph and intrinsic-tenase diagram showing factor VIIIa as the cofactor for factor IXa.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
World Federation of Hemophilia. Guidelines for the Management of Hemophilia.

questions.stem_html: A 49-year-old man has fatigue, early satiety, splenomegaly, leukocytosis with myelocytes and metamyelocytes, basophilia, and a low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score. The accompanying chromosome diagram shows a reciprocal translocation. Which molecular consequence drives this disorder?

options.text_html: Loss of a DNA mismatch-repair protein
Constitutive activation of a receptor serine-threonine kinase
Inactivation of both alleles of a retinoblastoma-family protein
Overexpression of cyclin D1 due to an immunoglobulin enhancer
Formation of a constitutively active BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase

questions.explanation_html: The Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) creates the BCR-ABL1 fusion protein, a constitutively active cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase that promotes proliferation and reduces apoptosis. It is the defining driver of CML and the target of ABL kinase inhibitors.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Mismatch-repair loss causes microsatellite instability in Lynch syndrome and some sporadic cancers.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: CML is not driven by a constitutively active serine-threonine receptor.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Biallelic RB-family loss is associated with retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma predisposition.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Cyclin D1 overexpression from t(11;14) is characteristic of mantle cell lymphoma.

questions.educational_objective: CML is driven by the Philadelphia chromosome, which creates the constitutively active BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase.

media.alt_text: Original chromosome 9 and 22 translocation diagram producing the BCR-ABL1 fusion kinase.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
WHO Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours: chronic myeloid leukemia, BCR::ABL1-positive.

questions.stem_html: A 27-year-old woman has painless cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, night sweats, and pruritus. Biopsy shows rare large binucleate cells with prominent nucleoli in a background rich in small lymphocytes, eosinophils, macrophages, and plasma cells. The accompanying schematic shows signaling from the large neoplastic cell to surrounding reactive cells. Which statement best describes this tumor?

options.text_html: The malignant cells are mature T cells that constitute nearly the entire mass
The malignant cells are myeloid precursors that secrete granulocyte colony-stimulating factor
The malignant cells derive from germinal-center B cells and recruit a prominent reactive microenvironment
The malignant cells are plasma cells that produce a monoclonal immunoglobulin spike
The malignant cells are natural killer cells with an obligate nasal distribution

questions.explanation_html: Classical Reed-Sternberg cells are crippled germinal-center B-cell derivatives that typically express CD15 and CD30. They are sparse within the node and secrete cytokines and chemokines that recruit the abundant reactive inflammatory cells composing most of the tumor mass.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma is not a mature T-cell neoplasm and malignant cells are usually rare.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Myeloid precursors characterize myeloid leukemias, not Hodgkin lymphoma.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Monoclonal plasma cells characterize plasma-cell myeloma.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma has a different phenotype and typical nasal involvement.

questions.educational_objective: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma contains sparse germinal-center B-cell-derived Reed-Sternberg cells that create a large reactive inflammatory microenvironment.

media.alt_text: Original diagram showing a Reed-Sternberg cell recruiting lymphocytes, eosinophils, macrophages, and plasma cells.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
WHO Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours: classical Hodgkin lymphoma.

taxonomy.subtopic: Third and fourth pharyngeal pouch failure

questions.stem_html: A newborn has truncus arteriosus, hypocalcemic seizures, and an absent thymic shadow. The accompanying embryology map highlights derivatives of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches. Abnormal development of which structures most directly explains the immune and calcium findings?

options.text_html: First pouch derivatives forming the auditory tube and middle ear
Second arch derivatives forming the stapes and styloid process
Neural crest cells forming the adrenal medulla only
Third and fourth pouch derivatives forming thymic and parathyroid tissue
Thyroglossal duct derivatives forming thyroid follicular cells

questions.explanation_html: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome disrupts development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, causing thymic hypoplasia with T-cell deficiency and parathyroid hypoplasia with hypocalcemia. Abnormal neural-crest contribution also produces conotruncal cardiac defects.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: First-pouch anomalies affect the middle ear rather than thymic and parathyroid development.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Second-arch derivatives do not explain T-cell deficiency or hypocalcemia.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Neural crest participates broadly in conotruncal development, but adrenal-medulla formation alone does not explain the syndrome.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Thyroid follicular cells arise from endoderm near the foramen cecum and are not the paired missing tissues here.

questions.educational_objective: 22q11.2 deletion causes thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia through abnormal third and fourth pharyngeal pouch development, often with conotruncal defects.

media.alt_text: Original diagram mapping third and fourth pharyngeal pouches to thymus and parathyroid glands.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
GeneReviews. 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome. NCBI Bookshelf.

questions.stem_html: A 4-month-old infant has persistent thrush, chronic diarrhea, recurrent viral and bacterial infections, and an absent thymic shadow. Both T- and B-lymphocyte counts are markedly reduced. The accompanying purine pathway shows deficiency of adenosine deaminase. Accumulation of which metabolite most directly impairs lymphocyte DNA synthesis?

options.text_html: Inosine, which inhibits thymidylate synthase
Uric acid, which blocks DNA polymerase
Deoxyadenosine-derived dATP, which inhibits ribonucleotide reductase
Adenylosuccinate, which inhibits purine salvage
Xanthine, which inhibits dihydrofolate reductase

questions.explanation_html: ADA deficiency causes deoxyadenosine and dATP accumulation. High dATP inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, reducing production of deoxyribonucleotides required for DNA synthesis and causing profound lymphocyte toxicity and SCID.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Inosine accumulation is not the toxic mechanism and thymidylate synthase is not the principal target.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Uric acid causes crystal disease rather than combined lymphocyte failure.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Adenylosuccinate does not explain ADA-deficient SCID.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Xanthine accumulation can occur in other purine disorders but does not inhibit dihydrofolate reductase in this syndrome.

questions.educational_objective: ADA deficiency causes SCID because deoxyadenosine-derived dATP accumulates and inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, impairing lymphocyte DNA synthesis.

media.alt_text: Original purine pathway showing ADA deficiency, dATP accumulation, and ribonucleotide-reductase inhibition.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
GeneReviews. Adenosine Deaminase Deficiency. NCBI Bookshelf.

questions.stem_html: A 72-year-old woman has progressive impairment of episodic memory and executive function. The accompanying membrane diagram compares two processing routes for amyloid precursor protein. Which enzymatic sequence produces the aggregation-prone peptide most strongly associated with extracellular plaques?

options.text_html: Alpha-secretase followed by caspase cleavage
Beta-secretase followed by gamma-secretase cleavage
Gamma-secretase followed by alpha-secretase cleavage
Lysosomal protease followed by ubiquitin ligase cleavage
Acetylcholinesterase followed by monoamine oxidase cleavage

questions.explanation_html: Amyloidogenic APP processing begins with beta-secretase cleavage and is completed by gamma-secretase, generating A-beta peptides including aggregation-prone A-beta 42. Alpha-secretase cleavage occurs within the A-beta sequence and prevents intact A-beta formation.

wrong_choice_explanations.3: The ordered amyloidogenic sequence begins with beta-secretase, not gamma-secretase.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Ubiquitin-proteasome pathways are not the defining APP cleavage route.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: These neurotransmitter enzymes do not process APP.

questions.educational_objective: Beta- then gamma-secretase cleavage of APP generates A-beta, whereas alpha-secretase cleavage is nonamyloidogenic.

media.alt_text: Original APP diagram contrasting alpha-secretase processing with beta- and gamma-secretase production of A-beta.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
National Institute on Aging. What Happens to the Brain in Alzheimer's Disease?

questions.stem_html: A 38-year-old man develops irritability, depression, involuntary dance-like movements, and difficulty planning tasks. His father developed similar symptoms at age 52, and his paternal grandfather was affected later in life. Imaging shows caudate atrophy. Which genetic event best explains the progressively earlier onset?

options.text_html: Maternal mitochondrial heteroplasmy
Loss of imprinting at chromosome 15
Somatic recombination of an immunoglobulin locus
Expansion of a CAG repeat during paternal transmission
Contraction of a CGG repeat during maternal transmission

questions.explanation_html: Huntington disease is caused by an expanded CAG repeat in HTT. Repeat length can increase during spermatogenesis, producing paternal anticipation with earlier onset and often greater severity in successive generations.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Mitochondrial inheritance is maternal and does not cause the autosomal dominant pattern shown.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Chromosome 15 imprinting disorders produce Prader-Willi or Angelman syndromes.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Immunoglobulin recombination is restricted to lymphocytes.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Fragile X involves CGG expansion, usually during maternal transmission, not contraction.

questions.educational_objective: Huntington disease demonstrates paternal anticipation due to expansion of the pathogenic HTT CAG repeat during spermatogenesis.

media.alt_text: Original diagram showing paternal CAG expansion across generations and caudate atrophy.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
GeneReviews. Huntington Disease. NCBI Bookshelf.

questions.stem_html: An 8-year-old girl has multiple daily episodes of sudden behavioral arrest lasting 10 seconds without postictal confusion. Hyperventilation provokes an event, and EEG shows generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges. The accompanying thalamocortical diagram highlights a low-threshold calcium current. Which drug action is most selective for this seizure type?

options.text_html: Irreversible inhibition of GABA transaminase
Use-dependent blockade of cardiac and neuronal sodium channels
Antagonism of NMDA receptors
Activation of presynaptic alpha-2 receptors
Blockade of thalamic T-type calcium channels

questions.explanation_html: Ethosuximide blocks low-threshold T-type calcium currents in thalamic neurons, disrupting the thalamocortical oscillation that generates generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave absence seizures.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Vigabatrin inhibits GABA transaminase and is used for selected seizure syndromes but is not the classic selective absence therapy.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Sodium-channel blockers can worsen some generalized absence epilepsies and are not the defining mechanism of ethosuximide.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: NMDA antagonism is not standard absence therapy.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Alpha-2 agonism produces sedation and sympatholysis rather than selective control of absence seizures.

questions.educational_objective: Ethosuximide treats childhood absence epilepsy by blocking T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons.

media.alt_text: Original 3-Hz spike-and-wave tracing linked to a thalamocortical T-type calcium-channel circuit.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
Glauser TA et al. Ethosuximide, valproic acid, and lamotrigine in childhood absence epilepsy. New England Journal of Medicine.

questions.stem_html: A farm worker develops diaphoresis, salivation, vomiting, wheezing, bradycardia, pinpoint pupils, muscle fasciculations, and weakness after pesticide exposure. Atropine is administered immediately. The accompanying enzyme diagram shows phosphorylation of acetylcholinesterase followed by a time-dependent structural change. Which additional treatment is most useful before that structural change occurs?

options.text_html: Pralidoxime, which can reactivate phosphorylated acetylcholinesterase before aging
Flumazenil, which antagonizes benzodiazepine receptors
Fomepizole, which inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase
Methylene blue, which reduces methemoglobin
N-acetylcysteine, which restores hepatic glutathione

questions.explanation_html: Organophosphates phosphorylate acetylcholinesterase. Pralidoxime removes the phosphate and restores enzyme activity if given before aging strengthens the organophosphate-enzyme bond. Atropine competitively blocks muscarinic receptors but does not reactivate the enzyme.

wrong_choice_explanations.3: Fomepizole treats methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning.

questions.educational_objective: Pralidoxime can reactivate organophosphate-inhibited acetylcholinesterase before aging; atropine blocks muscarinic effects but does not regenerate the enzyme.

media.alt_text: Original diagram showing acetylcholinesterase phosphorylation, pralidoxime reactivation, and time-dependent aging.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
CDC/ATSDR. Cholinesterase Inhibitors: Medical Management Guidelines.

questions.stem_html: A 20-year-old woman presents 10 hours after ingesting a large amount of acetaminophen. She has nausea and right upper-quadrant discomfort. The accompanying hepatic pathway shows normal conjugation routes and a minor cytochrome P450 route. Which action of N-acetylcysteine most directly reduces liver injury?

options.text_html: Competitive inhibition of alcohol dehydrogenase
Blockade of enterohepatic circulation
Irreversible inhibition of cytochrome P450 enzymes
Chelation of free iron within hepatocytes
Restoration of glutathione capacity for detoxification of NAPQI

questions.explanation_html: Acetaminophen overdose saturates glucuronidation and sulfation, increasing CYP-mediated formation of NAPQI. When glutathione is depleted, NAPQI binds hepatocellular proteins and causes centrilobular necrosis. N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione precursors and can also directly reduce the reactive metabolite.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Alcohol dehydrogenase inhibition is the action of fomepizole.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Interrupting enterohepatic circulation is not the antidotal mechanism.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: N-acetylcysteine does not irreversibly inhibit P450 enzymes.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Iron chelation treats iron overload, not acetaminophen poisoning.

questions.educational_objective: N-acetylcysteine prevents acetaminophen hepatotoxicity primarily by restoring glutathione-mediated detoxification of NAPQI.

media.alt_text: Original hepatic acetaminophen pathway showing conjugation, NAPQI formation, glutathione depletion, and N-acetylcysteine rescue.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
US FDA. Acetaminophen overdose and N-acetylcysteine treatment information.

questions.stem_html: A 17-year-old boy undergoes colonoscopy because his mother required colectomy at age 28. Hundreds of adenomatous polyps are present throughout the colon. The accompanying pathway shows a cytoplasmic complex that normally targets beta-catenin for degradation. Loss of which protein initiates this syndrome?

options.text_html: MLH1
SMAD4
RET
APC
VHL

questions.explanation_html: Familial adenomatous polyposis is caused by an autosomal dominant germline APC mutation. Loss of the remaining normal allele disrupts the beta-catenin destruction complex, allowing beta-catenin accumulation, nuclear Wnt-target transcription, and formation of numerous adenomas.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: MLH1 is a mismatch-repair protein associated with Lynch syndrome.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: SMAD4 loss is associated with juvenile polyposis and pancreatic cancer pathways.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: RET activation causes MEN2 and selected thyroid cancers.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: VHL loss stabilizes HIF in clear-cell renal carcinoma.

questions.educational_objective: FAP results from APC loss, which prevents beta-catenin degradation and activates Wnt-responsive proliferative transcription.

media.alt_text: Original pathway showing the APC destruction complex, beta-catenin degradation, and nuclear accumulation after APC loss.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
GeneReviews. APC-Associated Polyposis Conditions. NCBI Bookshelf.

questions.stem_html: A 52-year-old man has fatigue, bronze skin, diabetes mellitus, hepatomegaly, elevated transferrin saturation, and increased ferritin. The accompanying diagram shows iron transport from enterocytes and macrophages through ferroportin. Which regulatory abnormality most directly increases plasma iron?

options.text_html: Excess hepcidin causing ferroportin degradation
Inappropriately low hepcidin allowing persistent ferroportin-mediated iron export
Loss of transferrin synthesis causing impaired tissue iron delivery
Deficiency of ceruloplasmin causing isolated copper accumulation
Inhibition of divalent metal transporter 1 in duodenal enterocytes

questions.explanation_html: Most hereditary hemochromatosis causes inappropriately low hepcidin activity relative to body iron stores. Ferroportin remains on enterocytes and macrophages, increasing dietary iron absorption and iron release into plasma, producing high transferrin saturation and progressive tissue deposition.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Excess hepcidin reduces plasma iron by degrading ferroportin.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Low transferrin would not explain the classic high transferrin saturation and systemic loading mechanism.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Ceruloplasmin abnormalities involve copper metabolism or rare iron-handling disorders, not classic HFE hemochromatosis.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: DMT1 inhibition would decrease intestinal iron absorption.

questions.educational_objective: Hereditary hemochromatosis usually reflects inadequate hepcidin signaling, leaving ferroportin active and increasing intestinal and macrophage iron export.

media.alt_text: Original liver-enterocyte-macrophage diagram showing hepcidin control of ferroportin and systemic iron flow.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on haemochromatosis.

questions.stem_html: A 29-year-old woman with episodic headaches, palpitations, and hypertension is found to have bilateral adrenal medullary tumors. Her mother had medullary thyroid carcinoma. The accompanying pedigree and receptor diagram indicate autosomal dominant inheritance. Which molecular alteration is most likely?

options.text_html: Inactivating mutation of a nuclear DNA-repair protein
Loss of both alleles of a GTPase-activating protein
Activating germline mutation of the RET receptor tyrosine kinase
Expansion of a trinucleotide repeat in a transcriptional regulator
Inactivating mutation of the calcium-sensing receptor

questions.explanation_html: MEN2 is caused by autosomal dominant activating germline mutations in RET, a receptor tyrosine kinase. The syndrome includes medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma; MEN2A can also include primary hyperparathyroidism.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: DNA-repair defects produce other hereditary cancer syndromes such as Lynch syndrome.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Loss of a GTPase-activating tumor suppressor occurs in neurofibromatosis type 1.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Repeat expansions cause neurologic and neuromuscular disorders rather than MEN2.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Calcium-sensing receptor inactivation causes familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia.

questions.stem_html: A 40-year-old woman has weight loss, fatigue, orthostatic hypotension, salt craving, hyperkalemia, and diffuse hyperpigmentation involving the palmar creases and oral mucosa. Cortisol is low and ACTH is markedly elevated. The accompanying feedback diagram shows increased synthesis of proopiomelanocortin. Which mechanism causes the skin finding?

options.text_html: Increased aldosterone binding to melanocortin receptors
Accumulation of porphyrins within dermal macrophages
Deposition of iron in basal keratinocytes
Loss of sympathetic inhibition of eccrine glands
Increased POMC-derived ACTH and melanocortin peptides stimulating melanocytes

questions.explanation_html: Primary adrenal failure removes cortisol negative feedback from the hypothalamus and pituitary. POMC transcription rises, increasing ACTH and related melanocortin peptides. Their activity at melanocortin-1 receptors increases melanin production and causes diffuse hyperpigmentation.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Aldosterone does not stimulate melanocortin receptors and is deficient in primary adrenal failure.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Porphyrin accumulation causes photosensitivity, not this diffuse endocrine pattern.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Iron deposition can cause bronze pigmentation in hemochromatosis but does not explain high ACTH and hyperkalemia.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Sympathetic gland regulation is unrelated to POMC-associated pigmentation.

questions.educational_objective: Hyperpigmentation in primary adrenal insufficiency results from increased POMC-derived ACTH and melanocortin signaling after loss of cortisol feedback.
